highlights: Prebiotic fibers such as GOS, FOS, and inulin have the strongest evidence for supporting beneficial gut bacteria and microbiome diversity.
A diverse diet rich in fiber, plant foods, and fermented foods has a greater impact on gut health than supplements alone.
Probiotics can be beneficial, but their effects are strain-specific and do not consistently increase overall microbiome diversity.
Avoid products that promise to "reset" or "restore" the microbiome, as long-term gut health depends primarily on sustainable lifestyle and dietary habits.

blocks.text: What Is Gut Microbiome Diversity and Why Does It Matter?

Scientists call the microbiome the second human genome. It is a unique variety of bacteria concentrated mainly in the intestine. Each person’s microbiome is like a fingerprint. It is also increasingly referred to as another organ, like the heart or lungs. The intestinal microbiome consists of microorganisms that are mainly found in the gastrointestinal tract. Microbiome diversity is how many different microbes live in the gut. Scientists study this topic diligently, as it directly relates to our health. It depends on this diversity how resilient our bodies are to viruses and how well we feel every day. Thus, [low diversity was associated with higher rates of insulin resistance](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34110438/), HbA1c, and the inflammatory CRP marker in 506 people from the Northern Finland Birth Cohort and 1,140 TwinsUK participants.

Nutrition is one of the factors contributing to microbiome development. For instance, there are lots of fibers that are not broken down by our digestive system and are used as food for the bacteria residing in it. Thus, the consumption of a great variety of vegetable products contributes to the development of the microbial population, along with the use of fermented products like kombucha, kimchi, cottage cheese, and the like. However, it should be taken into consideration that the quantity of the microbial population is only one side of the coin.

Can Supplements Actually Improve Gut Microbiome Diversity?

It’s worth keeping an eye on the quality of your microbiome. Such factors as [your diet](https://www.biohackers.world/blog/biohacking-diet) and stress levels affect it, so discipline and constant monitoring are required. Of course, it may not seem easy in today’s realities of life. Therefore, bio-hackers are looking for other methods and means that will help make things easier and facilitate the diversity of the microbiome. Indeed, certain gut bacteria supplements can affect it; however, the efficacy of such influence varies greatly due to factors such as the ingredients, dosage, microbiome, nutrition, and the health of a particular person.
Best Gut Health Supplements for Microbiome Diversity

Let’s explore some of the most popular supplements for healthy gut bacteria. These are proven and studied supplements that will suit almost any healthy adult. Still, keep in mind that before taking digestive [health supplements](https://www.biohackers.world/blog/affordable-supplements-popular-in-the-biohacking-community), it is important to consult with a medical professional.
1. Prebiotic Fiber

They are substances that our body is not able to digest and are used as food sources by some bacteria in our gastrointestinal tract. There are several prebiotic substances that are useful for our gastrointestinal system; they include inulin, fructooligosaccharides (FOS), galactooligosaccharides (GOS), resistant starch, and partially hydrolysed guar gum (PHGG). They also affect the production of short-chain fatty acids. Prebiotic fibre might increase the amount of substrate for a microbe and alter the production of microbial metabolites. For example, in a randomized trial of 377 people with lactose intolerance, GOS [altered the composition of the microbiome and increased the number of fermenting bacteria](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8354614/).

items: Side effects: gas formation, swelling, and discomfort, especially with a rapid increase in dosage; the reaction is individual.
Who might be interested: people whose diets contain little fermentable fiber and have no contraindications to consuming it.
Evaluation of evidence: moderate-strong for altering individual components of the microbiome; moderate for specific increases in diversity.

blocks.text: 2. Psyllium Husk

If it’s tricky for you to obtain your daily ration of fiber, such a prebiotic supplement might be useful. It is a soluble fiber from the shell of seeds. Thanks to its absorbing properties, it fills the intestines and helps normalize GI function. It is believed that psyllium helps in the normalization of the stool and improvement of digestion. In a seven-day randomized psyllium study, the addition changed the composition of microbiota, with more significant changes and associated changes in acetone and propionate among participants. This shows the performance of this prebiotic additive. With regular use of psyllium, the microbiome environment can also potentially change, helping to enhance the immune response of the entire body. Be cautious about the amount of water you are drinking with psyllium; it should be about 1-2 glasses after the capsule.

items: Limitation: evidence for better digestion is much stronger than evidence for increased microbiome diversity.
Side effects: bloating, gas, and discomfort; psyllium should be taken with sufficient liquid.
Who might be interested: people who need extra soluble fiber or support for regular stools.

blocks.text: 3. Probiotics

If prebiotics are nutrition for bacteria, then probiotics come from other products. They interact with the gut, changing its microbial composition. But they do not necessarily attach to the gut. Even closely related bacteria have different sets of genes. So the effect of each probiotic depends on the strain. This way, one of the strains will work on your skin, and another is good for your stomach. Still, taking probiotic supplements doesn’t mean an instant change in your microbiome. The [efficacy of probiotics for gut health depends on both the specific strain and the disease or condition](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29868585/) for which it is used. Some show a result; others leave behind no change. Therefore, one inscription about the content of Lactobacillus is not enough.

items: Limitations: the effect depends on strain, dose, disease, and person; changes in overall diversity are not a reliable result.
Side effects: temporary gas and bloating are possible.
Target: people who choose a probiotic for a specific clinical purpose, for which there is research on the appropriate strain.

blocks.text: 4. Resistant Starch

This type of starch is not fully digested by the body. In the thick intestine, it becomes food for bacteria and is also fermented to form short-chain fatty acids, including butyrate. It is worth noting that although studies show a change in the presence of intestinal bacteria due to resistant starch, there is still a decrease in species diversity with its intake.

items: Limitations: results depend on the type of resistant starch, amount, and original diet.
Side effects: gas formation and swelling when consumption increases sharply.
The target audience is people who want to increase the amount of fermentable fiber in their diet.

blocks.text: 5. Fermented Foods / Postbiotic-Related Ingredients

Fermented foods are those that change their original appearance due to certain bacteria. This is often due to the fermentation process. These include: kefir, turpentine, kimchi, kombucha, etc. Probiotics, in turn, are a narrower concept referring precisely to the microorganisms that may be present in these products. Prebiotics are what we have previously called the substrate for microorganisms in our GI, and postbiotic is a drug made from non-living microorganisms or their components, for which there must be proven benefits to the organism. These are not interchangeable terms, but separate concepts.
6. Polyphenol-Rich Supplements

Polyphenols are compounds contained in berries, green tea, and turmeric. They also interact with bacteria and can potentially diversify your microbiome. Still, it is worth noting that, at the moment, studies do not show much change after taking a drug such as curcumin. Although there are distinct individual changes, it is impossible to say that they are of a mass nature. Yet scientists place considerable hope in polyphenols, as bacteria themselves can also convert them into other metabolites.

items: Limitations: results are highly dependent on the specific substance and form of the additive; a systematic review of clinical studies of berry polyphenols did not reveal convincing changes in the microbiome as a whole.
Side effects: gas, bloating, abdominal discomfort.
To whom it may apply: as an additional source of polyphenols, rather than as a primary tool for changing the microbiome.

blocks.text: 7. Omega-3 Fatty Acids

These are the beneficial fatty acids that help are quite a bit of multiskating for our body. They saturate the brain, help to form healthy nails and hair, and improve skin condition. However, they are not direct prebiotics for gut health. Omega-3 helps to diversify the number of bacteria, including Bifidobacterium, Roseburia, and Lactobacillus. But still, at the end of Omega-3 intake, the quality composition of the microbiome changed. It is therefore difficult to assert that Omega-3 is a necessary component for bacterial diversity. However, it can affect inflammatory processes in the body.

items: Limitations: data do not support a steady increase in overall microbiome diversity.
Side effects: some people may experience rashes, discomfort, or diarrhea.
To whom it may apply: people who need Omega-3 for other reasons, such as to make up for insufficient EPA/DHA intake, should not choose it solely for microbiome diversity.

What Actually Works Best for Gut Health?

Although the variability of gut health supplements today is quite extensive, there are still several other important factors that will help to support your body. Before focusing on the best gut health supplements, try to figure out your daily diet. For a diverse microbiome, your diet should also be diverse. Try to track how often you eat the same foods. Are your fruits and vegetables sufficient in your diet? Do you often consume fermented foods? Do you get the amount of fiber? Each of these factors ultimately has the most impact on your condition. If your diet is varied enough, but you still understand that certain components are missing, then it’s time to include supplements for microbiome diversity. Here’s a quick list of the main products that will help your body maintain a diverse microbiome:

items: Walnuts,
Whole grain products

blocks.text: In addition to nutrition, it is worth paying attention to factors such as daily stress levels and regular, healthy sleep. These parts seem unrelated to the health of the GI, but actually directly affect both it and the skin microbiome. To improve these indicators, you can look at physical activity. It reduces stress levels, normalizes hormonal status, and improves overall body health.

A separate point should be the administration of antibiotics. They kill the gut microbiome and require special supervision by a specialist. Remember, you can’t prescribe such drugs yourself; they must be prescribed by a doctor and given on prescription. Often, the diversity of our microbiota depends on these factors rather than on supplements.

blocks.text: How to Choose a Gut Health Supplement

To get the benefits of fiber supplements for gut health, it is important to understand how to use them correctly. Pay more attention to the composition of a package than to the brand itself. Sometimes, the names that are not the most well-known make it even better. Don’t forget to check the dosage, as it is quite individual. It’s best to count it together with a specialist. Don’t forget that even the best supplements for the gut microbiome will not replace a full diet, so you can use them as an extra tool but not count on them as a magic wand. Avoid brands that promise to deliver microbiome health instantly. Here is a small checklist to follow to improve the gut microbiome:

items: Look for clearly identified ingredients and strains.
Check the dose.
Check expiration/storage requirements.
Look for appropriate quality testing.
Avoid products making unrealistic claims.
Consider whether there is human evidence for the specific ingredient.
Don’t assume a larger ingredient list means better results.
Consider whether the supplement addresses an actual dietary or health need.

blocks.text: Common Mistakes When Taking Gut Health Supplements

In pursuit of a quick result, we can often overdo our time. It is therefore important to remember several basic rules associated with taking digestive health supplements. Do not take multiple products at the same time. This may cause undesirable outcomes in your gastrointestinal tract. It’s best to start with small doses and one component. Remember, more doesn’t mean better; take the dose you’re recommended. Research shows that probiotics work very individually due to the characteristics of each individual’s microbiome. Therefore, it is important to monitor your health during the introduction of a new rule. Also, do not ignore the features of your diet, as the basis of a healthy GI is formed on your plate.

Don’t wait for results immediately. The microbiome takes time to form and diversify, and it is difficult to say how long your own will last. Finally, it is important to distinguish improved digestive symptoms from a change in the microbiome. If the swelling or constipation has decreased after addition, it does not mean that the microbial diversity has increased or the structure of the microbiome has improved. Also, greater diversity does not always mean better health. It is not only the number and diversity of microorganisms that matter, but also their composition, function, and interaction with the body. Marketing promises such as: restores, reboots or repairs with a microbiome so evaluate especially critically.
How Long Does It Take to Improve Gut Health?

There is no clear answer to this question. Although the microbiome responds quickly to changes in nutrition, time is important for a stable picture. It all depends on your regular habits and consistent actions. It is important to understand that the speed and outcome of change also depend on what condition the digestive tract is in. The conditional term of changes is considered to be a few weeks to a month. Still, it is too individual a measure to give a specific time frame.

Your habits are also an important aspect. If you start eating a variety of foods, but over time return to the same food, the microbe will remain unchanged. The main factor in the diversity of your microbiome is you and how you eat permanently. To make this process easier and not go back to the starting point, try to build your diet a week in advance by prescribing products that will be in those 7 days. This will help you track the difference and understand what you are missing.

The Bottom Line — Which Gut Health Supplements Are Worth It?

As you can see, there are quite a few options for improving gut health. These include fermented products, probiotics and prebiotics, as well as special substances. Even though the idea that psyllium or similar prebiotic fibers will replace full-blown nutrition may be tempting, the basis of a healthy microbiome is your plate. And a conscious attitude towards nutrition. But gut microbiome diversity is not as complicated as it might seem at first. Trust only proven methods.
Best Supported

The most reliable facts and research are about prebiotic fibers. They show changes in the performance of GI and nutrition of bacteria found within them, especially GOS and FOS/inulin. The same applies to fiber that is not digested by our bodies, such as psyllium. However, you can also extract fiber from whole grains such as oatmeal, rice, or whole-grain bread. Don’t forget the fermented products; they help to enrich the germ. Excellent for curd, kefir, sauerkraut, or kimchi.
Promising

Let’s move on to promising but not sufficiently explored options. Resistant starch, polyphenols, and probiotic strains – all of which have been studied by scientists in a cursory manner but have not yet yielded stable results. Rather, very individual. This group can also include Omega-3. Although this component alone has proven to be beneficial for the human body, there is little evidence of long-term change or diversity in the microbiome.
Experimental

This group is the most undiscovered, and for now better to observe research on these components than to try them out themselves. For example, formulas for gut health. We don’t always know how the combinations of individual probiotics and prebiotics will work together in one capsule. If a product contains many components, it does not mean that they will improve the gut microbiome.

We can also include polyphenolic supplements. At the moment, this component is not thoroughly studied enough to spend money on it. The same applies to postbiotic formulas and additives with the label rebuild/reset/restore the microbiome. All products that promise big changes should be sidelined quickly. It is better to spend this money on a nutritious diet, which will diversify and increase your microbiome.
